meta.curriculum: National Curriculum Statement (NCS) - Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement (CAPS), FET Phase Grades 10-12
meta.notes: Primary source is the official CAPS FET Grades 10-12 policy document for each subject. Where the CAPS PDF text extraction was truncated (Physical Sciences Grades 11-12 detail; Life Sciences Grade 12 Term 3 tail), objective statements were taken from official DBE Annual Teaching Plans (2023/24 and 2024) and the DBE Grade 12 Examination Guidelines, which restate CAPS content. Gaps are flagged per topic where applicable.

objectives: Describe the basic structure and general characteristics of viruses, bacteria, protista and fungi (macroscopic protista and fungi mentioned only, not studied in detail)
Mention the roles these groups play in maintaining balance in the environment and web of life
Describe symbiotic relationships, including nitrogen-fixing bacteria in plants and E. coli in the human intestine

Discuss the effect and management of one disease from each group: viruses (rabies, HIV/AIDS, influenza), bacteria (blight, cholera, tuberculosis, anthrax), protists (malaria) and fungi (rusts, thrush, ringworm, athlete's foot)
Describe immunity, including plants' and animals' immune responses against infecting microorganisms, and vaccinations (briefly)
Discuss the use of drugs, e.g. antibiotics, and their effect on microorganisms
Describe the use of microorganisms to produce medicines (e.g. insulin and antibiotics)
Describe traditional technology using microorganisms to produce e.g. beer, wine and cheese

11.topic: Biodiversity of Plants and Reproduction in Plants
objectives: Group bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms according to the presence or absence of vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), true leaves and roots, seeds or spores, and fruit
Explain the decreasing dependence on water for reproduction from bryophytes to angiosperms
Compare asexual and sexual reproduction and name advantages and disadvantages of each
Describe flowers as reproductive structures and adaptations for pollination by wind, insects and birds (South African examples)
Discuss the significance of seeds: seed banks, seeds as a food source, and endemic species in South Africa
Show a basic understanding of phylogenetic trees as reconstructions of evolutionary pathways, and of cladograms, for the four plant groups
Explain the relationship between the body plan and the grouping of animals into phyla; the concept of a phylum
Study six phyla: Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda and Chordata
Describe key features of body plans: symmetry and cephalisation, number of tissue layers developed from the embryo, number of openings in the gut, coelom and blood systems
Relate body plans to modes of living for each of the six phyla, noting similarities and differences
Describe the role of invertebrates in agriculture and ecosystems (e.g. pollination, decomposition, soil aeration)

11.topic: Energy Transformations to Sustain Life: Photosynthesis
objectives: Describe the process of photosynthesis using words and symbols: intake of raw materials, trapping and storing of energy, formation of food in chloroplasts and its storage, and the release of oxygen
Mention only the light and dark phases (no biochemical details required)
Explain the importance of photosynthesis: release of oxygen, uptake of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and food production (trapping energy)
Discuss the effects of variable amounts of light, carbon dioxide and temperature on the rate of photosynthesis, using graphs
Explain the role of carbon dioxide enrichment, optimum light and optimum temperatures in greenhouse systems to improve crop yields
Describe the role of ATP as an important energy carrier in the cell
Compare dentition for herbivorous, carnivorous and omnivorous lifestyles in terms of nutritional requirements and energy relationships
Describe the macro-structure of the human alimentary canal and associated organs and the functions of the different parts
Explain the processes of ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion and the significance of each
Describe chemical digestion: functions of carbohydrases, proteases and lipases - where produced, substrate, pH and end-products
Describe absorption in the small intestine: adaptations to increase surface area, structure and significance of villi, and the importance of the hepatic portal system
Explain assimilation and the role of the liver: glucose metabolism, deamination of excess amino acids, and the breakdown of alcohol, drugs and hormones
Describe hormonal control of blood sugar levels and briefly explain diabetes

Discuss the importance of a balanced diet, changing requirements due to age, gender and activity, and malnutrition (kwashiorkor, marasmus, anorexia, bulimia, food allergies, coronary heart disease, diabetes and obesity)
Discuss the effects of alcohol and drug abuse, and tooth decay related to diet and fluoride in water supplies

11.topic: Energy Transformations to Sustain Life: Cellular Respiration
objectives: Describe aerobic respiration in the cytoplasm and mitochondria using words and symbols: glycolysis, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (no biochemical detail required)
Describe anaerobic respiration: production of lactic acid in muscles during exercise (words and symbols, no biochemical detail)
Discuss the role of anaerobic respiration in industry, e.g. beer brewing and bread making
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in terms of raw materials required, products and relative amounts of energy released
Distinguish between cellular respiration, breathing and gas exchange, and explain the need for gas exchange
List the requirements of efficient gas exchange organs: large surface area, thin, moist, well ventilated, protected, with a transport system
Briefly describe how these requirements are met in a dicotyledonous plant, earthworm, insect, bony fish and mammal
Describe the structure, location, adaptations and functioning of the human ventilation system: trachea, epiglottis, bronchi, bronchioles, lungs, ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm and alveoli
Explain ventilation of the lungs, gaseous exchange in alveoli and in tissues, the transport of gases around the body, and compare inspired and expired air
Briefly mention the homeostatic control of breathing
Describe causes, symptoms and treatment of TB in South Africa, and briefly study asthma, hay fever, bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer
Discuss the effects of smoking on gaseous exchange and smoking legislation in South Africa, and the effects of altitude on gaseous exchange
Briefly describe the role of the lungs, kidneys and bladder, liver, alimentary canal (gut) and skin in excretion, the substances excreted by each and their origins
Describe the structure of the urinary system: position of kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra
Describe kidney structure and functioning: removal of urea and excess water and salts, and reabsorption of glucose and some salts
Describe nephron structure and functioning: ultrafiltration, reabsorption, tubular excretion, pH control and the formation of urine
Explain homeostatic control of water and salts: the role of ADH and aldosterone
Discuss dialysis and kidney transplants, and mention diseases affecting kidney function (e.g. kidney stones, kidney failure, bilharzia infection)
Explain population size in terms of immigration, emigration, mortality and births; fluctuations, limiting factors and carrying capacity; logistic and geometric growth curves with phases
Describe predation using two South African examples of predator-prey relationships with graphs
Describe interspecific and intraspecific competition, ecological niches, and specialisation: competitive exclusion and resource partitioning with examples of coexistence
Describe parasitism, mutualism and commensalism, each with South African examples
Describe social organisation: benefits of herds/flocks (avoidance), packs (hunting), dominance and division of tasks (castes) (mention only)
Describe community change over time: primary and secondary succession and possible endpoints (mention only)

Discuss the human population: reasons for exponential growth, age and gender distributions for different countries including South Africa, and forecast South Africa's population growth with possible consequences for the environment

11.topic: Human Impact on the Environment: Current Crises for Human Survival
objectives: Discuss causes and consequences of atmosphere and climate change: carbon dioxide emissions, the carbon footprint and the need to reduce it, deforestation, the greenhouse effect and global warming (desertification, drought and floods), methane emissions and ozone depletion

Discuss water availability: construction of dams, destruction of wetlands, poor farming practices, droughts and floods, exotic plantations and depletion of the water table, boreholes and aquifers, wastage and the cost of water
Discuss water quality: pollution, diseases, eutrophication and algal blooms, the effect of mining, thermal pollution, and the need for water purification and recycling

Discuss food security: human exponential population growth, droughts and floods, poor farming practices (monoculture, pest control, loss of topsoil), alien plants, loss of wild varieties and impact on gene pools, genetically engineered foods and wastage
Discuss loss of biodiversity (the sixth extinction): habitat destruction, poaching (e.g. rhino horn, ivory, bush meat), and alien plant invasions with mechanical, chemical and biological control
Describe indigenous knowledge systems and the sustainable use of the environment, e.g. devil's claw, rooibos, fynbos, the African potato (Hypoxis) and Hoodia
Discuss solid waste disposal: managing dumpsites, the need for recycling, using methane from dumpsites for domestic use, and safe disposal of nuclear waste
Note: this topic must be completed in Grade 11 but is examined in both Grade 11 and the National Senior Certificate at the end of Grade 12
Describe the location of DNA in the cell: chromosomes, genes and extranuclear DNA (mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA)
Outline the discovery of the structure of DNA by Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins
Describe the structure of DNA: double helix of nucleotides with nitrogenous bases pairing A-T and G-C, deoxyribose sugar and phosphate
Explain the role of DNA: genes and non-coding DNA; DNA makes up genes carrying hereditary information and contains coded information for protein synthesis
Describe DNA replication in the cell cycle and its significance (the necessity for an exact copy)
Describe RNA: types (mRNA, tRNA), location in cells and structure
Explain protein synthesis: transcription from DNA and translation of RNA into proteins (mRNA, tRNA) as a sequence of events, with a basic understanding of the genetic code
Interpret DNA profiles (DNA fingerprinting) and state their uses
Describe meiosis as the process of reduction division and its purposes (gametogenesis, with exceptions such as mosses and ferns)
Explain the importance of meiosis: diploid to haploid; production of gametes; maintaining a constant chromosome number across generations
Describe the events of interphase and of each phase of Meiosis I and Meiosis II using diagrams, including crossing over in Prophase I and random arrangement of chromosomes at the equator
Explain the introduction of genetic variation through random segregation and crossing over
Describe the consequences of abnormal meiosis (non-disjunction), e.g. Down syndrome
Compare similarities and differences between mitosis and meiosis
Describe the diversity of reproductive strategies that maximise reproductive success in different environments, using appropriate animal examples
Distinguish between external and internal fertilisation
Distinguish between ovipary, ovovivipary and vivipary
Describe the amniotic egg
Distinguish between precocial and altricial development, and describe parental care
Describe the structure of the male and female reproductive systems and the functions of the parts
Describe the main changes at puberty under the influence of testosterone and oestrogen
Describe gametogenesis (spermatogenesis and oogenesis), related briefly to meiosis (no individual names of stages)
Explain the menstrual cycle with emphasis on hormonal control (FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone), including the ovarian and uterine cycles
Describe fertilisation and the development of the zygote to blastocyst
Describe implantation and development, gestation (briefly) and the role of the placenta
Define concepts of inheritance: genes and alleles, dominant and recessive, phenotype and genotype, homozygous and heterozygous; mention Mendel as the father of genetics
Solve monohybrid crosses with examples of complete dominance, incomplete/partial dominance and co-dominance
Solve dihybrid crosses involving phenotypes and genotypes
Explain sex determination, sex-linked alleles and sex-linked diseases (e.g. haemophilia and colour-blindness)
Solve genetics problems involving blood groups (multiple alleles)
Describe mutations: harmless, harmful and useful mutations; gene mutations and chromosomal aberrations, with links to natural selection
Interpret genetic lineages and pedigree diagrams
Discuss genetic engineering: stem cell research, genetically modified organisms, biotechnology and cloning
Describe paternity testing and DNA fingerprinting (forensics), and mention mitochondrial DNA in tracing genetic links

12.topic: Responding to the Environment: Humans (Nervous System and Sense Organs)
objectives: Explain that humans have two systems - nerves and hormones - that enable them to respond to the environment
Describe the central nervous system: meninges for protection; location and functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum, corpus callosum, medulla oblongata and spinal cord
Describe the location and functions of the peripheral nervous system and the autonomic nervous system
Describe the structure of a nerve and of sensory and motor neurons
Describe the structure, function and significance of a simple reflex arc, and the significance of synapses
Describe disorders (Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis), brain and spinal injuries (mention stem cell research), and the effects of drugs (dagga, heroin, ecstasy, tik)
Describe receptors detecting a range of stimuli: light, sound, touch, temperature, pressure, pain and chemicals (taste and smell)
Describe the structure and functioning of the human eye: binocular vision, accommodation, pupil reflex, and defects (short-sightedness, long-sightedness, astigmatism, cataracts)
Describe the structure and functioning of the human ear in hearing and balance, and hearing defects (deafness, middle ear infections, grommets)

Describe the location, hormones secreted and roles of hormones of the following glands: hypothalamus (ADH), pituitary gland (TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin, growth hormone), thyroid gland (thyroxin), pancreas (insulin, glucagon), adrenal gland (adrenalin, aldosterone) and gonads (oestrogen, progesterone and testosterone)
Distinguish between endocrine and exocrine glands
Explain examples of negative feedback mechanisms: TSH and thyroxin, and insulin and glucagon
Describe disorders caused by hormone imbalance, e.g. diabetes mellitus and thyroid disorders (goitre)
Describe homeostasis as the process of maintaining a constant, optimal internal environment
Explain negative feedback control of glucose, carbon dioxide, water and salts
Explain thermoregulation: adaptations of human skin, sweating, vasodilation and vasoconstriction
Describe the general functions of the plant hormones auxins, gibberellins and abscisic acid
Explain weed control by using growth hormones
Explain geotropism and phototropism and growth regulation by auxins
Describe plant defence mechanisms: chemicals and thorns
Discuss different kinds of evidence for evolution: the fossil record, modification by descent (homologous structures), biogeography and genetics
Explain the difference between a hypothesis and a theory
Give a brief overview of the history of different theories of development: Lamarckism, Darwinism and Punctuated Equilibrium

Explain Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection: variation in the gene pool, production of more offspring than required, environmental pressure, and survival and reproduction of better-suited organisms leading to extinction or successful adaptation
Describe artificial selection using one example of a domesticated animal and one example of a crop species
Distinguish between continuous and discontinuous variation, and describe sources of variation (crossing over, random arrangement of chromosomes, mutations, random fertilisation and random mating)
Explain speciation through geographic isolation, and the effect of speciation and extinction on biodiversity

Outline mechanisms of reproductive isolation that keep species separate: breeding at different times, species-specific courtship behaviour, adaptation to different pollinators, infertile offspring and prevention of fertilisation
Describe an example of natural selection and evolution in present times, e.g. insect resistance to insecticides, drug-resistant TB strains, HIV resistance to antiretrovirals, or Galapagos finches
Interpret a phylogenetic tree to show the place of the family Hominidae in the animal kingdom
Describe characteristics that humans share with African apes

Compare anatomical differences between African apes and humans: bipedalism (foramen magnum, spine and pelvic girdle), brain size, teeth (dentition), prognathism, palate shape, cranial ridges and brow ridges

Discuss lines of evidence for common ancestors of living hominids including humans: fossil evidence with evolutionary trends in Ardipithecus, Australopithecus and Homo, including fossil ages, sites (Cradle of Humankind) and the scientists who discovered them
Discuss genetic evidence (mitochondrial DNA) and cultural evidence (tool-making)
Explain the Out-of-Africa hypothesis - modern humans originated in Africa and migrated to other continents - and the fossil and genetic evidence supporting it
Interpret timelines for the existence of different species of the genus Homo and phylogenetic trees proposed by different scientists

12.topic: Human Impact on the Environment (examined in Grade 12)
objectives: Revise the Grade 11 topic Human Impact on the Environment (atmosphere and climate change, water availability and quality, food security, loss of biodiversity, solid waste disposal), which is examinable in the National Senior Certificate at the end of Grade 12
Term 4 is otherwise devoted to revision and preparation for the final NSC examination (Paper 1 and Paper 2, 150 marks and 2.5 hours each)

Physical Science.note: CAPS name: Physical Sciences. Six knowledge areas: Mechanics; Waves, Sound and Light; Electricity and Magnetism; Matter and Materials; Chemical Change; Chemical Systems. Detailed objectives below are from the official DBE Annual Teaching Plans (which restate CAPS content statements); topic outline and hours are from the CAPS overview of topics (Section 2.4).

objectives: Define a resultant and determine the resultant of vectors (maximum four) on a Cartesian plane using the component method
Sketch the net vertical vector (Ry) and net horizontal vector (Rx) on a Cartesian plane and sketch the resultant using the tail-to-head or tail-to-tail (parallelogram) method
Calculate the magnitude of the resultant using the theorem of Pythagoras and determine its direction using simple trigonometric ratios
Determine the resultant of two vectors graphically as well as by calculation for a maximum of four vectors in one and two dimensions
Explain the meaning of a closed vector diagram
Resolve a vector R into its horizontal and vertical components using Rx = R cos(theta) and Ry = R sin(theta)

11.topic: Newton's Laws and Application of Newton's Laws (Mechanics)
objectives: Define normal force, frictional force, static frictional force and kinetic frictional force; know that friction is proportional to the normal force and independent of contact area; solve problems using fs(max) = us N and fk = uk N
Draw force diagrams and free-body diagrams, and resolve a two-dimensional force (e.g. weight on an inclined plane) into parallel and perpendicular components
State Newton's first law of motion; define inertia and state that mass is a quantitative measure of inertia; discuss the importance of seatbelts
State Newton's second law of motion (Fnet = ma) and apply it to equilibrium and non-equilibrium problems: single objects on horizontal, inclined and vertical planes, with or without friction
Apply Newton's second law to two-body systems joined by a light inextensible string, including systems over a frictionless pulley
State Newton's third law of motion and identify action-reaction force pairs and their properties
State Newton's law of universal gravitation and solve problems using F = G m1 m2 / d^2
Calculate the acceleration due to gravity on Earth and on other planets; explain the difference between weight and mass; calculate weight using w = mg; explain weightlessness
Refraction of light
Snell's Law
Critical angles and total internal reflection

objectives: Wavefronts in two and three dimensions
Diffraction of waves

objectives: State Coulomb's law and solve problems using F = k Q1 Q2 / r^2 for charges in one dimension (restrict to three charges)
Solve Coulomb's law problems in two dimensions for three charges in a right-angled formation
Describe an electric field as a region in space in which an electric charge experiences a force
Draw electric field patterns for a single point charge, two point charges and a charged sphere
Define the magnitude of the electric field at a point as the force per unit charge (E = F/Q) and solve problems using this equation
Calculate the electric field at a point due to a number of point charges using E = kQ/r^2 (restrict to three charges in a straight line)
Use the Right Hand Rule to determine the direction of the magnetic field associated with a straight current-carrying wire, a single current-carrying loop and a solenoid
Draw the magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire, a current-carrying loop and a solenoid
Discuss qualitatively the environmental impact of overhead electrical cables
Define magnetic flux (phi = BA cos(theta))
State Faraday's law and describe what happens when a bar magnet is pushed into or pulled out of a solenoid connected to a galvanometer
Use the Right Hand Rule to determine the direction of the induced current in a solenoid, and know that the induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux
Calculate induced emf and induced current for a changing magnetic field using Faraday's law: emf = -N (delta phi / delta t)

11.topic: Electric Circuits: Energy and Power (Electricity and Magnetism)
objectives: State Ohm's law in words and interpret data and graphs of the relationship between current, potential difference and resistance at constant temperature
State the difference between ohmic and non-ohmic conductors and give an example of each
Solve problems using R = V/I for circuits with resistors in series and/or parallel (maximum four resistors)
Define power and solve problems using P = W/(delta t), P = VI, P = I^2 R and P = V^2/R
Use the energy relationships W = VQ, W = VI(delta t), W = I^2 R (delta t) and W = V^2 (delta t)/R
Deduce that the kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the use of 1 kilowatt of electricity for 1 hour (one unit of electricity) and calculate the cost of electricity usage

11.topic: Atomic Combinations: Molecular Structure (Matter and Materials)
objectives: Define a chemical bond, a covalent bond, a molecule, a bonding pair and a lone pair
Draw Lewis dot diagrams of elements and Lewis diagrams for simple molecules (e.g. H2, F2, H2O, NH3, CH4, HF) and molecules with multiple bonds (e.g. N2, O2, HCN)

Explain, in terms of electrostatic forces and energy, why two H atoms form an H2 molecule and why He does not form He2; interpret the potential energy versus distance graph for two approaching hydrogen atoms
Discuss molecular shapes: H2 (linear), H2O (angular), NH3 (pyramidal), CO2 (linear), CH4 (tetrahedral)
Describe the formation of the dative covalent bond
Define electronegativity; describe polar and non-polar covalent bonds with examples and show polarity using partial charges
Explain that bond character varies from non-polar covalent (delta EN = 0) to polar covalent (0 < delta EN <= 1,7) to ionic (delta EN > 1,7), and that polar bonds do not always lead to polar molecules
Define bond energy and bond length and explain the relationship between bond strength, bond length, size of bonded atoms and number of bonds
Describe the difference between intermolecular forces and interatomic (intramolecular) forces using diagrams and in words
Name and explain the different intermolecular forces (Van der Waals forces): mutually induced dipole (London) forces, dipole-dipole forces, dipole-induced dipole forces and hydrogen bonding
Describe ion-dipole forces between ions and polar molecules
State the relationship between intermolecular forces and molecular mass
Explain the effect of intermolecular forces on boiling point, melting point, vapour pressure and solubility
Relate the macroscopic properties of the three phases of water to its sub-microscopic structure (CAPS)

11.topic: Ideal Gases and Thermal Properties (Matter and Materials)
objectives: Describe the motion of individual gas molecules: collisions with each other and the container walls, and the range of molecular speeds
Explain the idea of average speeds in the context of gas molecules
Describe an ideal gas in terms of the motion of molecules, explain how a real gas differs from an ideal gas, and state the conditions under which a real gas approaches ideal behaviour

Describe the relationship between volume and pressure for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature (Boyle's law): practically, by interpreting results, using graphs and by writing a relevant equation
Explain the temperature of a gas in terms of the average kinetic energy of its molecules
Explain the pressure exerted by a gas in terms of collisions of the molecules with the container walls

11.topic: Quantitative Aspects of Chemical Change / Stoichiometry (Chemical Change)
objectives: Describe the mole as the SI unit for amount of substance, define one mole, and describe Avogadro's number as the number of particles in one mole
Define molar mass and calculate the molar mass of a substance given its formula
State Avogadro's law and know that the molar gas volume at STP is 22,4 dm3 per mol
Do calculations using n = m/M, n = V/Vm and n = N/NA, and interpret balanced equations in terms of volume relationships for gases
Define concentration and calculate it in mol per dm3 using c = n/V
Determine percentage composition, empirical formula and molecular formula of compounds
Do stoichiometric calculations including limiting reagents, percentage yield and percentage purity
Define heat of reaction (delta H), exothermic reactions and endothermic reactions
Classify reactions, with reasons, as exothermic or endothermic and state the sign of delta H for each
Define activation energy and activated complex
Draw or interpret fully labelled sketch graphs (potential energy versus course of reaction) of catalysed and uncatalysed endothermic and exothermic reactions

11.topic: Types of Reactions: Acid-Base and Redox (Chemical Change)
objectives: Write names and formulae of common acids (hydrochloric, nitric, sulphuric, ethanoic acid) and common bases (ammonia, sodium carbonate, sodium hydrogen carbonate, sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide)
Define acids and bases according to the Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry theories and identify conjugate acid-base pairs
Describe amphiprotic substances (ampholytes) and write equations showing how they act as acid or base
Write overall equations for reactions of acids with metal hydroxides, metal oxides and metal carbonates, and neutralisation reactions of common laboratory acids and bases
Describe acid-base indicators and know the colours of litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein and bromothymol blue in acids and bases
Explain the meaning of oxidation number and assign oxidation numbers to atoms in ions and molecules
Describe a redox reaction as involving electron transfer and changes in oxidation numbers, using the terms oxidation, reduction, reducing agent and oxidising agent
Balance redox reactions using half-reactions from the Table of Standard Reduction Potentials
The lithosphere: mining and mineral processing in South Africa
Energy resources and their uses

objectives: Define and calculate the momentum of a moving object (p = mv) and describe its vector nature
State Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum (Fnet = delta p / delta t) and calculate the change in momentum when a resultant force acts on an object
Define impulse and use the impulse-momentum theorem (Fnet delta t = m delta v) in one-dimensional calculations
Discuss impulse in relation to safety considerations (e.g. airbags, crumple zones)
State the principle of conservation of linear momentum; explain isolated system, internal and external forces
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions of two objects in one dimension
Distinguish between elastic and inelastic collisions by calculation

12.topic: Vertical Projectile Motion in One Dimension (Mechanics)
objectives: Explain what is meant by a projectile
Use equations of motion to determine the position, velocity and displacement of a projectile at any given time
Sketch position-time, velocity-time and acceleration-time graphs for free-falling objects, objects thrown vertically upwards or downwards, and bouncing objects
Determine position, displacement, velocity or acceleration at any time from given graphs, and describe the motion of an object from its graphs
Define the work done on an object and calculate the net work done, drawing force and free-body diagrams
Distinguish between positive and negative net work done on a system
State and apply the work-energy theorem on horizontal, vertical and inclined planes
Define conservative and non-conservative forces with examples
State the principle of conservation of mechanical energy and solve problems using Wnc = delta Ek + delta Ep
Define power, calculate power when work is done, and use Pave = F v(ave) for constant speed on rough horizontal or inclined planes
State the Doppler effect and explain, with illustrations, the change in pitch observed when a source moves towards or away from a listener (sound and ultrasound)
State applications of the Doppler effect with ultrasound in medicine, e.g. measuring the rate of blood flow or the heartbeat of a foetus
Solve problems using the Doppler equation fL = (v +/- vL)/(v +/- vs) fs when either the source or the listener moves
With light, explain red shifts and use the Doppler effect to explain why we conclude that the universe is expanding

12.topic: Electric Circuits: Internal Resistance and Series-Parallel Networks (Electricity and Magnetism)
objectives: Solve problems involving current, voltage and resistance for circuits containing resistors in series and in parallel (maximum four resistors)
Explain the term internal resistance
Solve circuit problems using emf = I R(ext) + I r, or emf = V(load) + V(internal resistance)
Solve problems with internal resistance for circuits containing series and parallel arrangements of resistors

12.topic: Electrodynamics: Electrical Machines and Alternating Current (Electricity and Magnetism)
objectives: State the energy conversion in generators and use the principle of electromagnetic induction to explain how generators work
Give examples of the uses of AC and DC generators and the functions of their components
State the energy conversion in motors and use the motor effect to explain how motors work; give examples of uses of motors
State the advantages of alternating current over direct current
Draw and interpret sketch graphs of voltage versus time and current versus time for an AC circuit
Define rms values for alternating voltage and current, and solve problems using Irms = Imax/sqrt(2), Vrms = Vmax/sqrt(2) and the average power relationships for a purely resistive circuit

12.topic: Optical Phenomena and Properties of Materials (Matter and Materials)
objectives: Describe the photoelectric effect and state its significance (it demonstrates the particle nature of light)
Define threshold frequency (f0) and work function (W0)
Perform calculations using the photoelectric equation E = W0 + Kmax, where E = hf and W0 = h f0 and Kmax = 1/2 m v(max)^2
Explain the effect of intensity and frequency on the photoelectric effect
Explain the formation of atomic spectra by referring to energy transitions and the difference between atomic absorption and atomic emission spectra

12.topic: Organic Chemistry: Organic Molecules (Matter and Materials)
objectives: Define organic molecules, functional group, hydrocarbon, homologous series, saturated, unsaturated and structural isomer

Write condensed, structural and molecular formulae (maximum 8 carbon atoms, one functional group per molecule) for alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols, haloalkanes, carboxylic acids, aldehydes, ketones and esters
Write IUPAC names from structural or condensed structural formulae and vice versa, identifying alkyl substituents (methyl and ethyl, maximum three)
Identify compounds that are saturated, unsaturated or structural isomers (chain, positional and functional isomers)
Relate physical properties (boiling point, melting point, vapour pressure) to the strength of intermolecular forces, type of functional group, chain length and branching
Describe the combustion of alkanes in excess oxygen and their use as fuels
Write the equation and reaction conditions for the formation of an ester and name the reactants and products

Classify organic reactions as elimination, addition or substitution, and write equations with reaction conditions for addition reactions of alkenes, elimination reactions (dehydrohalogenation, cracking, dehydration of alcohols) and substitution reactions (hydrolysis of haloalkanes, halogenation of alkanes)
Plastics and polymers

12.topic: Rate and Extent of Reaction (Chemical Change)
objectives: Define reaction rate and calculate reaction rate from given data
List the factors that affect the rate of chemical reactions
Explain in terms of the collision theory how the various factors affect the rate of chemical reactions
Answer questions and interpret data (tables or graphs) on different experimental techniques for measuring the rate of a given reaction
Define the term positive catalyst
Interpret graphs of the distribution of molecular energies to explain how a catalyst, temperature and concentration affect rate
Explain open and closed systems, reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
List the factors which influence the position of an equilibrium
State Le Chatelier's principle and use it to explain changes in equilibria
Interpret simple graphs of equilibrium
List the factors which influence the value of the equilibrium constant Kc, and write an expression for Kc from a given equation
Perform calculations based on Kc values and explain the significance of high and low values of the equilibrium constant
Define acids and bases according to Arrhenius and Lowry-Bronsted, and identify conjugate acid-base pairs
Distinguish between strong and weak acids/bases and between concentrated and dilute acids/bases
Write neutralisation reactions of common laboratory acids and bases, perform titration calculations and motivate the choice of an indicator
Determine the approximate pH of salts in salt hydrolysis
Explain the pH scale and calculate pH values of strong acids and strong bases
